clue.text: Brown's come outside, finds it hard to bear

indicators.note: one word standing outside another wraps around it, so the second word goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written; it splits around the other piece
umber is an earthy brown pigment; with the 's it becomes umber's

explanation.surface: Someone finds that a person called Brown coming out is hard to put up with.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown looks like a surname; it is the colour, as the pigment umber. C(UMBERS)OME.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cumbersome is heavy and awkward, so it is difficult to carry or bear.

clue.text: Prepare gun to shoot this pheasant ?

blocks.note: first meaning: to raise a firearm's hammer ready to fire
second meaning: a male bird, as in a male pheasant

explanation.surface: A shooter readies the gun to bag a game bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves seem to be one instruction about shooting a bird, but each defines the same word separately.
explanation.definitionFit: To cock a gun is to pull back its hammer before firing, and a cock pheasant is the male bird.

clue.text: Source of wealth, is not yours

blocks.note: first meaning: a pit dug to extract gold, coal or gems
second meaning: the possessive pronoun claiming something for oneself

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to share the fortune's origin with you.
explanation.definitionFit: A mine yields precious ore, and the pronoun 'mine' states ownership by the speaker rather than the listener.

clue.text: They should, on balance, prove successful

definitions.text: They should, on balance, prove successful

blocks.note: surface reading: taking everything into account, overall
setter's reading: literally standing on a tightrope or balancing pole, as acrobats do

explanation.surface: A cautious forecast that some people will, all things considered, do well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On balance' is an idiom for 'overall'; read literally it describes performers who keep their balance, and they succeed only by staying up.
explanation.definitionFit: Equilibrists are acrobats such as tightrope walkers whose whole act consists of keeping their balance.

clue.text: Clean up the undergrowth?

blocks.note: first meaning: to wash something by rubbing hard
second meaning: low stunted bushes and brushwood

explanation.surface: An instruction to tidy up the overgrown bushes in a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrub is to clean vigorously, and scrub is also low brushwood covering rough ground.

clue.text: Stern slim sort of 19

indicators.note: a sort of something is a loose version of it, so these letters are rearranged into another form

blocks.note: the letters of both words together

explanation.surface: A description of a severe, thin musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' does double duty: it shuffles the first two words and, with 19, defines the answer as a kind of musician.
explanation.definitionFit: Minstrels were medieval singers and players, a type of musician, the answer to 19 across.

clue.text: Care to amend the measure?

indicators.note: amending something alters it, so these letters are put into a changed order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician asks whether anyone would like to revise the proposed bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' sounds like a parliamentary bill; here it is a unit of land area.
explanation.definitionFit: An acre is a unit of land area, one of the imperial measures.

clue.text: His is a hard case

blocks.note: surface reading: a tough, difficult person or problem
setter's reading: a rigid outer shell protecting an animal's body

explanation.surface: Someone's situation is described as a tough one.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'hard case' is a tough nut of a person; literally it is the shell of a crab or lobster.
explanation.definitionFit: Crabs, lobsters and shrimps belong to the group of animals with hard jointed shells called exoskeletons.

clue.text: I represent a different undertaking

indicators.note: making something different changes its form, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words together

explanation.surface: A lawyer or agent says they act for some other venture.
explanation.definitionFit: An enterprise is a project or business venture, something a person sets out to do.

clue.text: Agreeing to run together

blocks.note: first meaning: in accord, of the same opinion
second meaning: happening or running at the same time, from Latin for running together

explanation.surface: Two people consent to go jogging with each other.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Latin concurrere, to run together, so the second half is its literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Concurrent opinions coincide, and concurrent events or prison sentences run simultaneously alongside one another.

clue.text: About the last form of worship

blocks.note: c. is short for circa, Latin for about
ult. is short for ultimo, last month, in old business letters

explanation.surface: A remark about the final style of religious service.
explanation.walkthrough: C for circa and ULT for ultimo are standard abbreviations, the latter once common in commercial letters ('your letter of the 5th ult.').
explanation.definitionFit: A cult is a system of religious devotion directed at a particular figure or object.

clue.text: Business in which interest is disappearing ?

definitions.text: Business in which interest is disappearing

blocks.note: surface reading: a firm whose profits or returns are dwindling away
setter's reading: interest means concern, and disappearing means going, so a concern that is going

explanation.surface: A company whose returns to investors are shrinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests failure, but a going concern is a business that is actively trading; the clue reads concern for interest and going for disappearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Going concern is the accounting phrase for a business that is operating and expected to keep trading.

clue.text: Sightseer taking the round trip

blocks.note: surface reading: a journey out and back again
setter's reading: a trip around the round thing, the whole planet

explanation.surface: A tourist buying a return ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round trip' sounds like a return journey; the round thing is the world itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A globetrotter is a person who travels widely all over the world, often as a tourist.

clue.text: Latitudinarian clergy? That's the stuff!

blocks.note: a latitudinarian is tolerant and liberal in belief, broad-minded, as in the Broad Church
the cloth is a collective term for the clergy

explanation.surface: An exclamation that liberal churchmen are just what is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's the stuff!' sounds like hearty approval; stuff is an old word for woven fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcloth is a fine woollen or cotton fabric, and stuff is an old general word for woven material.

clue.text: A word of little significance

blocks.note: surface reading: an unimportant word
setter's reading: a word that signifies littleness, such as booklet or piglet

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark about a trivial word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of little significance' means unimportant, but here it means a word that signifies something little.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar a diminutive is a word formed to express smallness, such as duckling from duck.

clue.text: Make up for lost time, if time is money

definitions.text: Make up for lost time, if time is money

blocks.note: surface reading: work harder to catch up after a delay
setter's reading: swap money in for time, and it becomes making up for lost money

explanation.surface: A busy worker's resolution to catch up, with the proverb that time is money.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb lets the solver replace time with money, turning catching up into paying back someone's losses.
explanation.definitionFit: To reimburse is to repay a person money they have spent or lost.

clue.text: The old master makes his mark during a term break

indicators.note: a broken word is smashed and its parts reassembled in another order
something happening during a period falls within it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: the article belongs to the surface; the word term supplies the letters to be rearranged
a brand is an identifying mark, such as one burnt into a hide

explanation.surface: A famous painter becomes known during a school holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Term break' reads as a half-term holiday between school terms, but break is the signal to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt was the great 17th-century Dutch painter, one of the Old Masters of European art.

clue.text: Part of Venice ? Rialto, to be more precise

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is taken, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one name and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Someone asking which part of Venice, and answering the Rialto to be exact.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rialto is the old commercial district of Venice. Nice in its old sense means fine or exact, as in a nice distinction.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice in its older sense means finely discriminating or exact, so the comparative means more exact.

clue.text: Tony Weller's recommended defence

blocks.note: surface reading: a character's advice about how to protect oneself
setter's reading: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers, Tony Weller cries that Mr Pickwick's lawyers should have pleaded a 'alleybi'

explanation.surface: A literary character's advice on how to win a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Weller, Sam Weller's father in Dickens's Pickwick Papers, laments at the breach-of-promise trial: 'Vy worn't there a alleybi!'
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a plea that the accused was somewhere else when the crime happened, a standard legal defence.

clue.text: Work is play to them

blocks.note: surface reading: people who enjoy their jobs so much it feels like leisure
setter's reading: their job is literally to play instruments, and a work is a composition

explanation.surface: A description of lucky people who love their jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: Play here means performing music, and a work is a piece of music they play.
explanation.definitionFit: Musicians are people who play instruments or perform music professionally.

clue.text: Passwords for shop assistants ?

blocks.note: surface reading: secret phrases letting staff into somewhere
setter's reading: notices or signs placed on a shop counter, where assistants stand

explanation.surface: A question about the secret codes given to shop staff.
explanation.walkthrough: A countersign is a military password; split, it suggests signs on a shop counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A countersign is a secret word or signal given in reply to a sentry's challenge, a password.

clue.text: In confectionery it's simply topping

blocks.note: surface reading: old British slang praise, simply splendid
setter's reading: it is just the layer on top of a cake

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic verdict on some sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' was British slang for excellent; here it is literally what goes on top of a cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Icing is the sugary coating spread over the top of cakes and biscuits.

clue.text: The old country, to a certain degree, is backward

indicators.note: going backward means reading from the end to the start, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: MA is a Master of Arts degree
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that some former nation is somewhat behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To a certain degree' looks like 'somewhat', but the degree is an academic one.
explanation.definitionFit: Siam is the former name of Thailand, changed in 1939, so it is an old country name.

clue.text: One vote in favour, or more ?

definitions.text: One vote in favour, or more

blocks.note: surface reading: a single yes vote
setter's reading: the plural of that yes vote, as counted in a division of Parliament

explanation.surface: A tally of support at a meeting: one in favour, perhaps several.
explanation.walkthrough: One yes vote is an aye; more than one makes the plural, as when the Speaker says 'the ayes have it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayes are votes cast in favour, or the members voting yes in a parliamentary division.

clue.text: " Empty " describes this poet's own metamorphosis

indicators.note: a metamorphosis is a change of shape, so the letters are transformed into a new arrangement

blocks.note: void means empty

explanation.surface: The word 'empty' sums up how a poet changed himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is apt: the Roman poet Ovid wrote the Metamorphoses, a poem about transformations.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovid was the Roman poet of the Augustan age, author of the Metamorphoses and the Art of Love.

clue.text: Does this call for treatment by a faith-healer?

definitions.text: Does this call for treatment by a faith-healer

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who cures illness through prayer or belief
setter's reading: someone who mends broken faith, so the ailment is unfaithfulness

explanation.surface: A question whether some condition needs a spiritual healer.
explanation.walkthrough: A faith-healer heals by faith; read the other way, it heals faith, and a lack of faith or fidelity is the complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Infidelity is unfaithfulness, especially to a spouse, and also disbelief in a religion.

clue.text: The mark of Paris, the cad

blocks.note: first meaning: Paris of Troy shot Achilles in his one vulnerable spot, the back of the foot
second meaning: a dishonourable, untrustworthy man

explanation.surface: A rogue is identified by his Parisian style.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris is the Trojan prince, not the city, and his mark is what he aimed at: Achilles' heel.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend Paris killed Achilles with an arrow to the heel, and heel is also slang for a scoundrel.

clue.text: They're assumed for dramatic effect

blocks.note: surface reading: put on or pretended, for show
setter's reading: taken on by actors working in the theatre

explanation.surface: Some poses are struck just to impress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dramatic effect' suggests showing off; read literally, it is the theatre, where performers take on new identities.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage names are professional pseudonyms adopted by actors and performers.
